dedupe_keys.name: tree caused distribution outages at a virginia electric utility retrospective case series of 844 failures musick and co authors auf 2026

description: This case study analyses the trees that caused power outages on the distribution network of a Mid-Atlantic electric utility in Virginia. Cindy Devlin Musick, Ida Holásková, Michael Strager, Charlene Kelly, Paul Kinder, Gregory Dahle and Matthew Walker of West Virginia University published it in Arboriculture & Urban Forestry in June 2026, with the utility's urban foresters investigating over 1,104 outages. For each outage the team recorded on a mobile app the tree type, genus, diameter and height, prior defects and health, and whether roots, stem or branches failed; 844 complete records were tested with chi-square, Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel and polytomous logistic regression. Most outages came from live trees failing at the trunk, 46% had no visible defect, and branch failure was unlikely overall but more frequent in yellow poplar and maple than in pines. Coverage is one utility's service area. Format and access: an article free to read on the journal site. Licence: copyright of the International Society of Arboriculture. Caveats: the outage records themselves are not released. It informs vegetation management and storm resilience of overhead lines. Related catalogue records are the Washington DC street tree inventory, which records overhead wires, and the Noord-Brabant urban tree wind damage study.
